top_level_objectives: Use Lewis structures to determine the number of electron domains around a central atom.
Apply VSEPR theory to predict electron-domain geometry and molecular shape.
Distinguish between bonding pairs and lone pairs and explain how lone pairs affect bond angles.
Compare VSEPR predictions with the observed shapes of common molecules.

scenes.scene_name: Introducing VSEPR from a Lewis Structure
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the core idea that electron pairs around a central atom repel one another and adopt an arrangement that minimizes repulsion.
key_visuals: A simple Lewis structure with a highlighted central atom
Floating electron domains around the atom gradually spreading apart
A label emphasizing bonding pairs versus lone pairs
student_actions: Identify the central atom and count electron domains
Predict how the domains should arrange themselves
Trigger the geometry to settle into the lowest-repulsion arrangement

scenes.brief_purpose: Build the five fundamental electron-domain geometries as the foundation for all later molecular shapes.
key_visuals: Side-by-side models of linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements
Angle markers showing ideal bond angles
A simple domain counter tied to each geometry
student_actions: Match each electron-domain count to the correct geometry
Rotate the models to inspect their 3D arrangement
Compare ideal angles across the five cases

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how replacing bonding domains with lone pairs changes the visible molecular geometry while preserving the underlying electron-domain arrangement.
key_visuals: A tetrahedral arrangement changing into bent and trigonal pyramidal examples
A trigonal bipyramidal arrangement changing into seesaw and T-shaped forms
An octahedral arrangement changing into square pyramidal and square planar forms
student_actions: Remove or add lone pairs to see the resulting shape change
Identify the molecular geometry for each electron-domain arrangement
Explain why the shape name differs from the electron-domain geometry

scenes.scene_name: Comparing Repulsion Strengths and Angle Changes
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain why lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs and how that leads to compressed bond angles.
key_visuals: Visual cues showing lone pairs as larger or more diffuse regions of electron density
A comparison between ideal and observed bond angles
Water and methane shown side by side with their different angles
student_actions: Compare angles in molecules with and without lone pairs
Infer which repulsions are strongest from the visual evidence
Relate angle compression to lone-pair repulsion

scenes.scene_name: Case Studies: Water, Ammonia, Methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4
scenes.brief_purpose: Connect VSEPR predictions to real molecules students are likely to encounter in chemistry.
key_visuals: Each molecule displayed with its Lewis structure and 3D shape
Labels indicating electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry
A simple checklist showing predicted versus observed geometry
student_actions: Predict the geometry for each molecule before revealing the answer
Compare predictions with the displayed molecular model
Classify each molecule by electron domains and shape

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate the full VSEPR workflow from Lewis structure to 3D shape and reinforce common shape patterns.
key_visuals: A flow diagram from Lewis structure to electron-domain geometry to molecular geometry
A mixed set of molecules for quick review
A final summary of the five geometries and common derived shapes
student_actions: Work through a short sequence of practice predictions
Check answers and correct any mismatches
Summarize the steps used to solve VSEPR problems
